questions.prompt: Who stands on the straight line from YOU toward the net?
questions.explanation: Gold 1 shares the centre lane between the puck and the attacking net.

questions.prompt: Choose two ways to investigate a different shooting opportunity.

options.text: Assume the puck must go through Gold 1
Check whether D2 has a usable connection

questions.explanation: Moving or passing may change the lane; this picture alone does not prove a shot will reach the net.

questions.prompt: Order one response to the blocked point lane.

options.text: Use the option that remains available

questions.explanation: A player may choose a pass, carry or shot depending on the next cue.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare a lateral shooting angle.
questions.explanation: A small lateral change shifts the line to the net. Check whether Gold 1 can follow before treating it as open.

questions.prompt: Suppose Gold 1 follows your lateral move. What deserves another look?

options.text: The original shot as though Gold 1 had stayed still
A shot without checking the blocker
A pass to D2 or another change of angle

questions.explanation: A moving defender can close the new lane, so alternatives remain relevant.

questions.prompt: Why does “move sideways” not guarantee a clear shot?
questions.explanation: Explain that the blocker, other players and goalie can also adjust.

questions.prompt: Which teammate can give YOU a lateral puck option if Gold 1 stays in the shooting line?
questions.explanation: D2 is the Navy teammate positioned for a lateral option, so moving the puck can change Gold 1’s screen; if D2 is covered, keep the blocker in the read.

questions.prompt: Which two changes could alter the shooting picture?
questions.explanation: A lateral puck option or changed screen can alter the line; shooting through the blocker ignores the visible constraint.

questions.prompt: Move YOU laterally to create a different sightline from the puck.
questions.explanation: The lateral position changes the screen and may open D2’s route; if Gold 1 follows, the new lane must be checked.

questions.prompt: Why does a blocker make the read about geometry rather than simply shooting harder?
questions.explanation: Gold 1 occupies the direct line, so angle, screen and support determine what is visible; if those do not change, more force does not create a lane.

questions.prompt: Which player is the new puck carrier?
questions.explanation: The puck is now assigned to F2 after the stated pass.

questions.prompt: Which two reads help before reoffering?

options.text: Whether the return pass is guaranteed
The space available beyond your old spot

questions.explanation: A give-and-go needs a real route and a prepared carrier, not just a memorized pattern.

questions.prompt: Arrange one reoffer routine.
questions.explanation: The route should change if the defenders remove the expected opening.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to illustrate a new inside option for F2.
questions.explanation: Moving into different ice changes the passing picture. The reference is only useful if Gold 2 and Gold 1 cannot remove that route.

questions.prompt: If Gold 2 moves into your new route, what could you do?

options.text: Change direction or stay as another support option
Insist on the return pass anyway

questions.explanation: The pass does not obligate the receiver to return it; another support action may be better.

questions.prompt: How can you judge whether your second movement improved the play?
questions.explanation: Look for a new useful route, space created for F2 or a defender moved—not only whether you received a return pass.

questions.prompt: What can YOU call to make F2 aware of your reoffer?

options.text: Inside option when you can see me
The first pass is still coming
No need to look at pressure

questions.explanation: The call names a new inside option while leaving F2 to confirm the lane; if Gold 1 tracks the route, re-space before asking for the puck.

questions.prompt: Which two cues should drive your second movement?
questions.explanation: The new carrier location and defender orientation shape the return lane; staying fixed can leave you behind pressure.

questions.prompt: Move YOU inside and slightly lower to create another visible option for F2.
questions.explanation: The new angle gives F2 a short release and changes Gold 1’s line; if the defender tracks, rotate to another support lane.

questions.prompt: How can YOU tell a reoffer is helping instead of just following the puck?
questions.explanation: It should change the passing angle and preserve separation from Gold 1, while keeping another teammate useful; if it closes every lane, re-space.

questions.prompt: From which side is Gold 1 closest to YOU?
questions.explanation: Gold 1 is at a less negative y value, toward the middle of the ice.

questions.prompt: Pick two checks before turning with the puck.

options.text: Room and support after the turn
A promise that a turn always beats the defender

questions.explanation: Protection should preserve a next action rather than simply hide the puck.

questions.prompt: Order a possible protective read.

options.text: Check the space for a turn
Protect possession and look for the next option

questions.explanation: Actual edge control and reach require on-ice instruction; this is a decision routine.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to illustrate space for a protective reset.
questions.explanation: A retreat toward available ice may buy room, but the boards and following pressure limit it.

questions.prompt: If F2 becomes clearly available while Gold 1 closes, what might be useful?

options.text: Consider moving the puck before the space disappears
Carry into Gold 1’s approach by default

questions.explanation: A pass can be an alternative to protection if its route and receiver are ready.

questions.prompt: What next option would make a protective turn useful here?
questions.explanation: A new passing route, room to carry or time to scan—not the turn itself as an end goal.

questions.prompt: Which teammate can become a reachable outlet after the protective turn?
questions.explanation: F2 is the Navy teammate inside and visible as the outlet, so protection can lead to a connected pass; if Gold 1 closes F2’s lane, keep protecting until another route appears.

questions.prompt: Which two cues should precede a protective turn?
questions.explanation: Pressure side and support lane decide where the puck can be protected and released; faceoff history does not.

questions.prompt: Move YOU closer to the boards while keeping F2 visible inside.
questions.explanation: The wall-side spot shields the puck from Gold 1 and preserves F2’s lane; if F2 is covered, continue protecting or reset.

questions.prompt: When does a protective turn become a possession play rather than just avoiding contact?
questions.explanation: It buys time while keeping a reachable outlet visible, allowing the next action; if no lane opens, protection should continue until support changes.

questions.prompt: Which player is between the puck carrier and the defending net?
questions.explanation: YOU are closer to Navy’s net than Gold 1 and are the closest shown defender to that net.

questions.prompt: Which two things would you need before deciding how quickly to close?

options.text: A fixed gap that suits every attacker

questions.explanation: Distance alone cannot determine a safe closing action; speed and support are missing or changing.

questions.prompt: Arrange a read before managing this gap.

options.text: Adjust while keeping a useful defensive position

questions.explanation: The routine is conditional; the still image cannot measure the speed needed.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to another example position between Gold 1 and the net.
questions.explanation: The reference preserves net-side position. Whether retreating this far is useful depends on actual speed and support.

questions.prompt: With C back alongside Gold 1, which two checks help you defend together?

options.text: Reassess whether you still need to cover the rush alone
Stop tracking Gold 2 because C has returned
Communicate which threat C can help cover

questions.explanation: Recovering help can change responsibilities, but communication and the second attacker still matter.

questions.prompt: Why is the drawn distance insufficient to prescribe an exact gap?
questions.explanation: Include skating speed, direction, pressure and support; none can be fully proved by one still picture.

questions.prompt: Who is the closest shown defender to Navy’s net?
questions.explanation: YOU is drawn between Gold 1 and the Navy net, so inside protection is first; if C arrives, communicate the next assignment.

questions.prompt: Which two cues should change your closing distance?

options.text: A fixed distance rule regardless of the play

questions.explanation: Carrier lane and support position determine a useful close; a fixed rule ignores the scene’s changing options.

questions.prompt: Move YOU slightly inside Gold 1’s route while keeping C’s recovery lane visible.
questions.explanation: The inside position protects the net and leaves C a readable recovery route; if Gold 1 passes, switch to the new carrier.

questions.prompt: How does C’s recovery change your job without prescribing a fixed gap?
questions.explanation: C’s position can provide help or require YOU to contain longer, so read the carrier and support together; if C is late, protect the middle.
